Vibration stick feeding · for tube-packaged components on the JUKI RS-1

Components arrive in sticks. They should feed like tape.
Four lanes. One lock. No hand-picking bench.

The S-JVF02 is a four-channel vibration stick feeder engineered for the JUKI RS-1 feeder bank. Tube- and stick-packaged components — from 3 × 3 mm up to 30 × 10 mm — load into 66 mm lanes, vibrate smoothly to the front of the tube, and present themselves to the placement nozzle at a repeatable height and attitude. Lift the handlebar, aim at the alignment hole and connector, release to lock: the feeder is online in four steps.

01 — Why it matters

Tube-packaged parts are where a pick-and-place line quietly loses hours

Resistors, diodes, connectors, small transformers and many odd-form parts still ship in sticks and tubes — packaging that protects long leads and fragile bodies but defeats tape feeding. Without a stick feeder, an operator hand-picks them one by one: slow, inconsistent, and the single most common source of wrong-part and reversed-polarity escapes on high-mix lines. The S-JVF02 turns that bench into a machine step that runs at the placement cycle.

01

Hand-picking is the hidden bottleneck

Every stick-packaged component placed by hand costs seconds the machine could spend placing. Multiply by boards per shift and the 'small' parts decide your real output — and nobody logs it because the mounter was never the constraint.

02

Manual feeding escapes errors

A person loading parts from a stick tray can invert polarity, mix adjacent values, or fatigue by hour six. A vibration lane presents one part at a time, at one height, in one attitude — the nozzle either picks the right part or the machine alarms.

03

Changeovers burn uptime

Without multi-lane feeding, every extra part number means another feeder slot, another stop, another qualification. Four independent channels let one S-JVF02 carry four part numbers — or hold a deep stock of one high-runner so lanes are swapped, not the machine stopped.

02 — The method

From stick to nozzle in six repeatable moves

Stick feeding is older than SMT, but the engineering is in the details: how the tube is held, how hard it shakes, and how the part stands when the nozzle arrives. The S-JVF02 sequences it into six steps, all documented in the product manual.

01

Load the lanes

Component sticks slide into the four channels. Each lane is independent, so you can run four different part numbers on one feeder — or four sticks of the same part to keep the pick area supplied for longer.

02

Lock onto the bank

Installation is a four-move sequence from the manual: put up the handlebar, aim at the alignment hole, aim at the connector, release the handlebar and the feeder is locked in the RS-1 feeder bank. No tools, no shimming, no re-tramming.

03

Fix and tension the tube

The rear end of the tube rests above the support frame and is fixed by the locating ring; the middle sits under the leaf spring under pressure; the front end is fixed by the locating piece, and the top face of the tube is cut off at the nozzle picking area. Three points, one defined pick height.

04

Dial the vibration

Power on, then set frequency and power on the control unit dials until components travel smooth and speedy toward the pick area — the manual's own words. Too little and parts stall; too much and they bounce out of attitude. Two dials cover the whole material world from 3 × 3 mm to 30 × 10 mm.

05

The nozzle picks

The RS-1 nozzle descends into the opened pick area and lifts the leading component. Because the tube is fixed at the locating piece and the parts are presented in a known attitude, the pick height and offset stay the same on cycle one and cycle fifty thousand.

06

Replenish without stopping

As parts are consumed, vibration carries the column forward and the pick area stays full. When a lane empties, you slide in the next stick — the other three lanes keep feeding, and the line keeps placing.

Step sequence and fixturing details are quoted from the S-JVF02 product manual (installation and set-up chapters).

Built around the parts list — serviceability as a design goal

Handlebar + lock, no tools

The handlebar carries the whole mounting operation: lift, aim, seat, release. The same mechanism that locks the feeder to the bank is what a competitor would need three screws and a gauge for.

Three-point tube fixturing

Locating ring at the rear, leaf spring in the middle, locating piece at the front. The tube is defined at three points, so pick height does not drift as lanes empty and refill.

Leaf spring under documented pressure

The middle of the tube rides under the leaf spring 'and being in the pressure' — the manual's own setup rule — which damps bounce and keeps components in attitude during high-frequency runs.

Guide rail and support frame

Injection-moulded guide rails and a rigid support frame keep the four lanes parallel and the sticks aligned to the nozzle path, lane after lane.

Modular control unit

Frequency dial, power dial, pilot lamp and switch sit on a single control unit (part S-JVF02-052805) — one module to stock, one module to swap.

Every part numbered

The manual publishes a 14-item part list with part numbers from S-JVF02-052801 (main body) to S-JVF02-052814 (connector). Order by number, swap in minutes, keep no line down.

Two dials and a lamp — controls an operator actually uses

Frequency dial

Sets how fast the lane shakes. Light parts and long parts want different frequencies; the dial covers the material window without a parameter manual.

Power dial

Sets how hard the lane shakes. Together with frequency it is the whole tuning procedure: 'test and get the correct frequency and power setting to run components smooth and speedy'.

Pilot lamp + switch

The lamp says the lane is live at a glance from the aisle; the switch kills power for lane changes without touching the bank supply.

Bank connector

Power and communication arrive through the standard RS-1 feeder bank connector the moment the handlebar locks — plug-and-play is a mechanical fact here, not a slogan.

06 — Installation

Four moves onto the bank, five steps to tune

The product manual defines the whole commissioning: a four-step mechanical install and a five-step set-up. Plan for minutes, not hours — and have the component sticks on hand for the tuning run.

STEP 1 · Unbox and inspect

Check the main body, handlebar, control unit and the locating parts against the 14-item part list in the manual. Confirm the lane guide rails are clean and the leaf spring is in place.

STEP 2 · Put up the handlebar

Manual installation step 1: raise the handlebar to its open position. It is the lever that will draw the feeder home into the bank.

STEP 3 · Aim at the alignment hole

Manual installation step 2: seat the feeder against the RS-1 bank alignment hole. This — not shims or gauges — defines the machine-side position.

STEP 4 · Aim at the connector, then lock

Manual installation steps 3 and 4: align the connector, release the handlebar and the feeder locks in the feeder bank. Power and communication are now live through the bank.

STEP 5 · Fix the tube

Set-up steps 1 to 3: the end of the tube above the support frame fixed by the locating ring; the middle under the leaf spring and in pressure; the front end fixed by the locating piece, then cut off the top face of the tube at the nozzle picking area.

STEP 6 · Power on and tune

Set-up steps 4 and 5: power on, then test and set frequency and power until components run smooth and speedy. Log the two dial positions per part number — your next changeover starts from a known setting.

ARTICLE 01Tube-packaged components are where your line quietly loses hours

The mounter is never the bottleneck — the bench where someone hand-picks stick-packaged parts is. Here is the invisible cost chain and a five-minute audit that exposes it.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-JVF02 product manual and product document.

Walk the length of a busy SMT floor and you will find the bottleneck in the same place in almost every factory: not at the mounter, but beside it, at a small table where an operator is picking components out of plastic tubes with their fingers.

Stick-packaged parts — resistors, diodes, small connectors, anything with long leads or a body too awkward for tape — arrive in packaging that was designed for protection, not for automation. So the line absorbs them the expensive way: seconds per part, by hand, all day. Nobody logs it because the mounter was never the constraint. The constraint is the bench, and the bench is invisible on the capacity spreadsheet.

Here is the five-minute audit. Pick your three highest-volume stick-packaged parts. For one shift, count how many are hand-picked, time the pick-and-place per part with a phone stopwatch, and multiply by your monthly board volume. Then ask the second question: how many wrong-part or reversed-polarity escapes came from that bench last quarter? The first number prices the labour; the second prices the risk.

Once the bench has a number, the alternative is simple to specify. The S-JVF02 locks onto the JUKI RS-1 feeder bank and runs four independent lanes of 66 mm sticks, presenting components from 3 × 3 mm up to 30 × 10 mm to the placement nozzle at a fixed height and attitude. Two dials — frequency and power — tune the flow; the tube is fixed at three points so nothing drifts. Fifteen watts of vibration replaces a shift of hand-picking.

The compounding part: once stick parts are machine-fed, they enter your normal planning world. Cycle counts become real, changeovers get logged, and the bench's variability leaves your quality conversations. The next product introduction that ships in sticks stops being a staffing problem — the lanes are already running.

Run the five-minute audit this week. Then send us the three part numbers, a photo of the sticks and the number you found — info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576 — and we will tell you, honestly, whether a stick feeder pays for your mix or whether hand-picking is still the right answer.

ARTICLE 02The four-lane question: how much changeover is your RS-1 paying for?

Every extra part number can cost a slot, a stop and a re-qualification. What four independent channels actually buy you in changeover minutes — and when they don't.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-JVF02 product manual and product document.

There is a quiet tax on every high-mix line, and it is levied every time the product changes: the changeover. Slots get re-planned, feeders get re-qualified, and the mounter — the most expensive machine on the floor — waits.

Think about what a stick-packaged part does to a changeover on a JUKI RS-1. One part number usually means one lane of attention: load, position, tune, verify. Multiply by four part numbers and you have four setups, four failure points, and four chances for yesterday's setting to be lost when the next operator takes the shift.

The reusable method is to count setups, not slots. Ask: across one week of production, how many distinct stick-fed part numbers does the line need, and how many setup events do they cause? A single-lane feeder answers with one setup per part per change. A four-channel feeder answers with setups you can prepare and label — because the channels are independent, part A can keep running while part B's lane is loaded and tuned off-cycle.

The S-JVF02 was built around exactly this arithmetic: four input channels on one 365 × 66 × 125 mm body, each with its own tube fixturing — locating ring, leaf spring, locating piece — and its own frequency and power tuning. Mounting the feeder itself is four tool-less moves on the bank: handlebar up, alignment hole, connector, release to lock. The setup you log today is the setup you recall next week.

Keep a dial-setting card per part number at the bank, and review it quarterly with your volumes. Factories that do this stop treating stick parts as artisanal work: the changeover becomes paperwork, and paperwork does not stop machines.

If your week is full of stick-fed changeovers, send us your part list and volumes. We will map it to a lane plan — which parts share a feeder, which run deep stock, which need the custom geometry service — before you spend anything.

ARTICLE 033 × 3 to 30 × 10: the component window a stick feeder covers

The size window sounds narrow until you inventory against it. How to check which of your 'manual only' parts were automatable all along.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-JVF02 product manual and product document.

"Our parts are special" — every feeder salesperson on earth hears this, and about half the time it is true. The other half is an inventory nobody has measured against a published window.

The S-JVF02's window is printed in the product document: components from 3 × 3 mm up to 30 × 10 mm, on sticks 66 mm wide. That sounds narrow until you run your real list against it. Horizontal resistors and diodes: inside. Small electrolytics and film caps: inside. Connectors, optocouplers, small transformers with bodies under the window: inside. The parts you currently hand-pick are overwhelmingly the parts that fit — they simply arrived in protective packaging that no one automated.

Here is the method: export your component master, filter for package type = stick/tube, and sort by annual placements. The top of that list is your automation queue, ranked by the money you already spend on it. The parts below the window — the ones that genuinely do not fit — get their own honest line, and that line is where custom design starts.

For the parts inside the window, the feeder does the rest. Each of the four lanes holds the tube under a leaf spring and presents components to the nozzle through the opened pick area; frequency and power dials adapt the flow to the part's weight and friction. For the parts outside it, the documented five-day customized design service adapts lane geometry and fixturing to the component — the same way the S-JVF02 itself was designed for the RS-1 bank.

Re-run the export every time the planner adds a part family. The list is a living document, and the top ten rows are a roadmap: they tell you which feeder to buy next, not which one you happen to be missing today.

Send us your filtered list — sizes and annual placements are enough. We will mark each row feed-standard, feed-custom, or honestly 'keep it manual', with the reason.

ARTICLE 04Frequency, power, leaf spring: the three settings that stop jams

A repeatable tuning method for vibration feeding — too little shakes parts loose, too much shakes them out of attitude. The dial discipline that fixes both.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-JVF02 product manual and product document.

Every vibration feeder on the floor obeys the same physics, and every jam is one of two sentences: the part stopped moving, or the part moved too much.

Too little vibration and the column stalls before the pick area: the nozzle descends onto an empty tube, the machine errors, someone taps the feeder — the universal gesture of manual intervention — and the cycle time you planned evaporates. Too much and parts bounce: they ride over each other, stand up in the lane, or present at an angle the nozzle cannot pick. The jam you see is at the pick; the cause you missed is three components back.

The method the S-JVF02 manual encodes is three fixturing points and two dials. Fix the tube first: the rear end above the support frame held by the locating ring, the middle under the leaf spring and 'in the pressure', the front end fixed by the locating piece with the top face cut off at the nozzle picking area. A tube that is not defined at three points cannot be tuned — the geometry moves under you. Then set frequency to make the parts travel, and power to keep them in attitude; the manual's own acceptance test is that components run 'smooth and speedy'.

Dial positions are settings, so treat them like recipes. Write the two numbers per part number on the lane card, and re-verify after any spring or ring change — a new leaf spring changes the pressure, and the pressure changes the tuning. This one habit removes most of the 'random' jams, because they were never random.

Keep the tuning card at the machine and audit it when a new product arrives. Within a quarter you will have a small library of settings — the operating knowledge that used to live in one technician's head, now written down where shifts cannot lose it.

If your parts sit outside the smooth-and-speedy window — too light, too sticky, too long-leaded — tell us what happens at the pick. That is exactly the case the five-day custom design service exists for.

ARTICLE 05Plug and play is a mechanical promise: alignment hole, connector, handlebar

Why feeder accuracy is decided by geometry, not by the technician's patience — and what 'no tools, no gauges' really means on a bank changeover.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-JVF02 product manual and product document.

'Plug and play' is the most overused phrase in factory automation. On a feeder bank it has one honest meaning: the machine knows exactly where the feeder is, every time, without a technician arguing with it.

Consider what happens without that guarantee. A feeder mounted on shims and hope sits at a slightly different height every time; the nozzle's pick offset learns the difference as wear; and the first unexplained pick error of the week is blamed on the component, the vacuum, the weather — anything but the two millimetres nobody measured. Every 'mystery' escape traces back to geometry.

The S-JVF02 answers with three mechanical facts published in its manual. The alignment hole defines where the feeder sits on the bank — the same datum the machine expects. The connector defines where power and communication come from, and it can only go in one way. The handlebar does the clamping: lift it, seat the feeder, release it, and the lock pulls the body against its datum. No tools, no gauges, no second opinion. Installation is four moves and they are in the manual in that order.

That geometry is what makes the rest of the promise work. Because the feeder is located, the tube fixturing is located: locating ring, leaf spring, locating piece. Because the tube is fixed at three points, the cut-open pick area presents components at the same height on cycle one and cycle fifty thousand. The pick repeatability people attribute to 'tuning' is mostly just geometry that was never allowed to move.

Test your own bank the same way: mount, remove, remount, and check whether anything had to be adjusted between runs. If something did, that adjustment is a hidden setup time you pay on every changeover — and it is exactly what a located, handlebar-locked feeder removes.

Want the drawings? The stick feeder 3D model and the product manual are linked on this page, and our engineers will check them against your bank layout before you order.

ARTICLE 06What 15 watts buys against an operator's shift

The energy maths is a rounding error; the labour maths is the business case. A four-line comparison of machine-fed versus hand-picked stick components.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-JVF02 product manual and product document.

An operator's shift costs a number you pay every month and rarely divide. A fifteen-watt feeder costs a number you will find on an electricity bill in about four years of rounding.

Put the two side by side. Hand-picking a stick-packaged component is a reach, a grasp, a move, a placement, a check — call it three to eight seconds of skilled attention per part, repeated thousands of times, degrading as the shift wears. The machine version: the lane presents the part, the nozzle takes it, the cycle counter adds one. The energy cost of that presentation is 15 W at 24 V DC, per the S-JVF02 product document — the whole feeder draws less than the monitor on your line supervisor's desk.

This is not a comparison of machines against people; it is a comparison of what each is good at. Hands are brilliant at irregular work and terrible at being a queue. A person who spends a shift feeding stick parts is a quality inspector, a kitter and a problem-solver reduced to a metronome — and the metronome slows down at hour six.

The arithmetic that makes the case concrete takes four inputs: stick-pack components per board, boards per day, your own stopwatch time per hand placement, and your loaded wage. The calculator on this page runs exactly those four lines with your numbers and nothing pre-baked, so you can show it to your CFO without a salesperson in the room.

Then watch the second-order effects over a quarter: the pick errors that used to arrive from the bench, the lane that kept feeding during the changeover, the training conversation that stopped being about dexterity. The watts stay fifteen; the savings compound.

Run the four lines with your numbers this week. If the answer surprises you, send us the inputs — we will tell you what the same feeder does on your worst part and your best day.

ARTICLE 07The fourteen parts between you and a stopped line

A published part list is a maintenance strategy. How numbering every wear part — spring, ring, piece, connector — turns downtime into a two-minute swap.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-JVF02 product manual and product document.

A stopped line is never waiting for a motor. It is waiting for the small mechanical part that took the vibration trade for ten thousand cycles — and for someone to know its name.

Open the S-JVF02 product manual and you find an unusual thing for a device this simple: a fourteen-item part list, every line numbered, from S-JVF02-052801 (main body) to S-JVF02-052814 (connector). Top plate, leaf spring, control unit, spring, handlebar, support frame, locating piece, front cover, vibrator, locating pin, guide rail, locating ring. That list is not paperwork; it is a maintenance strategy printed in advance.

Here is how to use it. Identify the wear items — the parts that live under pressure and motion: the leaf spring that holds the tube, the locating ring and piece that define it, the connector that mates a thousand times, the control unit with the dials your operators touch. Keep one of each per feeder bank on the shelf. When a lane misbehaves after the tuning check, you are not diagnosing a mystery; you are swapping a numbered part in minutes.

The reason this works on a stick feeder specifically is the design itself: modular fixturing, a bolt-in control unit, a tube path you can see. A feeder whose wear parts are buried inside a sealed assembly gets replaced; a feeder whose wear parts are on a published list gets kept. Keeping is cheaper — and the documented one-day spare parts lead-time means 'cheaper' also means 'today'.

Review the list every time you add a part family to the lanes. New geometry, new spring pressures, new wear patterns — the shelf stocking is a living decision, and the fourteen numbers make it an easy one.

Need the list as a stocking plan? Send us your feeder count and bank layout; we will turn the fourteen part numbers into a shelf inventory with quantities, and quote the kit with the feeders.

ARTICLE 08Before you automate stick feeding, run these four numbers

A payback method with your own volumes, your own time study and your own price — plus the three savings the method deliberately leaves out.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-JVF02 product manual and product document.

Most payback conversations about small automation are dishonest in the same direction: the vendor's spreadsheet finds savings you will never collect. Here is the opposite method — four lines, your numbers, and a bias toward under-claiming.

Line one: what does the bench cost today? Count the stick-pack components per board, the boards per day, and the seconds per hand placement you measured yourself — not the number from a brochure, your number. Line two: what does the feeder actually take over? Be honest: it automates the repeatable picks, not the weird ones. Use the share your process really allows. Line three: your loaded wage and your working days. Line four: divide the quoted feeder price by the annual labour the first three lines freed. If the answer is under twelve months, this is a financial decision, not a capital debate.

The calculator on this page runs those four lines exactly, with nothing pre-baked. No invented time studies, no competitor-bashing multipliers, no price hard-coded anywhere — every money figure is typed in by you.

Now the three savings the method deliberately leaves out, because they are yours to prove: the escapes a manual bench lets through — wrong part, reversed polarity, the component that was pushed in at an angle and failed at reflow; the machine slot a four-lane feeder frees on a crowded bank; and the training cost of the bench itself, which is really the cost of every new hire learning your parts with their fingers.

Every factory that starts measuring stick-fed labour finds it was hiding in someone else's cost line — usually 'consumables' or 'overtime'. The four lines make it visible, and visible is negotiable.

Send us the four numbers. We will turn them into a lane configuration — channels, spare kit, tuning cards — and a quotation that matches the arithmetic you already trust.

What components can the S-JVF02 actually feed?
Stick- or tube-packaged components from 3 × 3 mm up to 30 × 10 mm, on 66 mm sticks: resistors, diodes, small capacitors, connectors and many odd-form parts. If your part ships in a stick today, it is very likely inside the window — send a sample stick and we will confirm the presentation.
Does it fit any machine other than the JUKI RS-1?
The S-JVF02 as published is engineered for the RS-1 feeder bank — standard alignment hole and connector. The same vibration-stick principle is customized for other mounters in our feeder family (the catalogue covers feeding for 'ANY SMT machines'); tell us the platform and we quote the interface variant.
How fast can it feed? What throughput should I plan?
The lane presents parts faster than the RS-1 nozzle can take them — throughput is set by the machine's pick cycle, not the feeder. The feeder's job is to never starve the nozzle: four channels, one high-runner lane lasting roughly four times longer than a single-lane stick, and tuning that keeps flow 'smooth and speedy'.
What happens when a component jams?
Most jams are tuning, not hardware: frequency too low (parts stall) or power too high (parts bounce out of attitude). The manual's set-up procedure — fix the tube at three points, then dial frequency and power — eliminates the structural causes. The leaf spring keeps the tube under pressure so it cannot walk loose.
What are the power and utility requirements?
24 V DC at 15 W, delivered through the standard RS-1 feeder bank connector the moment the handlebar locks. No compressor, no external supply, no software licence.
What spare parts should I stock?
The manual publishes a 14-item part list (S-JVF02-052801 to -052814). The wear items to keep on the shelf are the leaf spring (052802), locating ring (052808), locating piece (052813), control unit (052805) and connector (052814). With the documented 1-day spare parts lead-time, most factories keep one of each per feeder bank.
How long does installation and changeover take?
Mounting is four moves: put up the handlebar, aim at the alignment hole, aim at the connector, release to lock — seconds, with no tools. A lane changeover is sliding a new stick in and recalling the logged dial settings. The full commissioning, including tuning, is a same-shift job.
How do I get a quotation?
Send a photo of your component sticks, the sizes, the board volumes and your machine list to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 13602562576. You get a lane configuration, a spare part kit proposal and a price — usually within one working day, with a sample feeding test available before you commit.
